QUESTION: Which hypertension-associated metabolites show a statistically significant positive
correlation with systolic blood pressure specifically within the 'Bread-spiker' phenotypic group,
after adjusting for age and BMI? List the top 10 metabolites passing significance and direction.

ANSWER
======

Bread-spiker definition (as specified): per-subject mean bread-meal peak glucose rise
(peak post-meal glucose - pre-meal baseline, averaged over replicates) computed only from plain
Bread meals (all Bread+Fat / Bread+Protein / Bread+Fiber preload meals excluded).
Cohort median = 56.5 mg/dL (37 subjects with plain-bread CGM data)
=> 18 of 37 subjects are bread-spikers (mean 75.4 +/- 20.5 mg/dL) vs 19 non-spikers (39.6 +/- 12.9).
14 of the bread-spikers also have metabolomics, age, BMI and systolic BP and form the tested
group: XB20, XB21, XB33, XB42, XB59, XB62, XB68, XB70, XB79, XB94, XB100, XB101, XB107, XB111
(SBP 91-146 mmHg, mean 119.8; age 25.2-79.0 y; BMI 20.7-34.4 kg/m2).

Model: one OLS regression per metabolite, SBP ~ metabolite + age + BMI, n = 14, metabolite
predictor = log10 replicate-averaged abundance, z-scored across subjects (units = mmHg per 1 SD).
Tested 974 metabolites: 115 reached p < 0.05; 49 of these had a POSITIVE coefficient.

TOP 10 METABOLITES (positive and p < 0.05, ranked by p; beta = mmHg per +1 SD of log10 abundance,
adjusted for age and BMI; partial r = age/BMI-adjusted correlation)

 1. cis-4-Hydroxyproline      (6.63_130.0513m/z)  beta = +11.61 mmHg, t = 6.21, p = 1.0e-4, r = 0.891
 2. Proline                   (8.14_157.0968m/z)  beta = +10.50 mmHg, t = 4.75, p = 7.8e-4, r = 0.833
 3. Proline (CE10 adduct)     (8.14_115.0633n)    beta = +10.27 mmHg, t = 4.54, p = 1.07e-3, r = 0.821
 4. Citrinin                  (4.77_250.0802n)    beta = +10.67 mmHg, t = 4.49, p = 1.16e-3, r = 0.818
 5. Asp-Arg (dipeptide)       (13.04_290.1453m/z) beta = +16.09 mmHg, t = 4.16, p = 1.95e-3, r = 0.796
 6. Kynurenic acid            (4.28_190.0496m/z)  beta = +10.84 mmHg, t = 3.99, p = 2.55e-3, r = 0.784
 7. Pro-Phe (dipeptide)       (6.91_262.1340n)    beta = +10.14 mmHg, t = 3.86, p = 3.16e-3, r = 0.774
 8. N-Acetylgalactosaminitol  (5.88_222.0987m/z)  beta =  +9.70 mmHg, t = 3.86, p = 3.18e-3, r = 0.773
 9. Medazepam                 (11.62_271.1031m/z) beta = +16.48 mmHg, t = 3.72, p = 4.01e-3, r = 0.761
10. Creatinine                (0.54_114.0663m/z)  beta = +14.06 mmHg, t = 3.45, p = 6.18e-3, r = 0.738

KEGG/HMDB where annotated: cis-4-hydroxyproline C01157; proline C00148/HMDB00162; kynurenic acid
C01717/HMDB00715; Asp-Arg HMDB28747; Pro-Phe HMDB11179; creatinine C00791/HMDB00562.
Ranked 11-15 for context: bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (+9.90, p=7.7e-3), threonine (+9.51,
p=8.0e-3), second proline feature 0.55_116.0707m/z (+9.30, p=9.5e-3), second creatinine feature
2.85_112.0519m/z (+12.92, p=1.07e-2), D-malic acid (+8.79, p=1.19e-2).

THE MOST CREDIBLE SIGNAL
The proline / 4-hydroxyproline axis. Proline is annotated on six features (four with positive
coefficient and p < 0.05), and the strongest hydroxyproline feature has the smallest p-value of all
974 tests. The signal replicates across independent LC-MS features, and it is the only metabolite
group that survives every sensitivity analysis: alternative pre-meal baselines (mean of -25..-5 min,
the -5 min sample, or the pre-meal minimum), peak windows of 120/150/170 min, median computed over
the 27 metabolomics-covered subjects (median 60.1 mg/dL, 13 spikers), log10/log1p/raw transforms,
mean vs median replicate aggregation, and a per-sample model with n = 55 replicate-level
observations (in that model cis-4-hydroxyproline p = 3.4e-9, proline p = 1.6e-8, both at FDR
q < 0.05). It also remains the lead after adding sex as a covariate.

CAVEATS (important)
- No metabolite survives Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across the 974 tests in the primary n = 14 model
  (minimum q = 0.093 for cis-4-hydroxyproline; 0 features at q < 0.05, 2 at q < 0.10). The list
  above is a nominal-p (p < 0.05) screening result, not an FDR-significant set: under the global
  null ~49 of 974 features would reach p < 0.05 by chance (comparable to the 115 observed) and ~6
  would reach the top-10 cutoff p <= 6.2e-3. The rank order and the cross-feature replication of
  the proline/hydroxyproline signal, not the p-value flag itself, carry the evidence.
- n = 14 (bread-spikers with metabolomics + complete age/BMI/SBP); 4 of the 18 bread-spikers lack
  metabolomics and 4 more lack BMI or SBP. Effect sizes are not clinically calibrated at this n.
- Several top hits are likely mis-annotations or drug/xenobiotic artefacts rather than endogenous
  hypertension metabolites: medazepam (a benzodiazepine), citrinin (a mycotoxin), and
  bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate should not be interpreted biologically. More than half of the
  metabolome table carries `Discard` or placeholder annotations (16% flagged Discard, 39%
  placeholder); restricting to `Discard == "Keep"` leaves proline, Asp-Arg, kynurenic acid,
  Pro-Phe and creatinine as the higher-confidence subset.
- Associations are cross-sectional (SBP cannot be shown to be caused by these metabolites), and
  residual confounding by medication, renal function, sodium intake and muscle mass is possible;
  medication-related drug metabolites correlate with blood pressure by construction.
- Biological interpretation is hypothesis-generating: proline/4-hydroxyproline point to collagen
  turnover and extracellular-matrix remodelling (arterial stiffening), Asp-Arg, ornithine,
  citrulline and homoarginine to arginine/nitric-oxide metabolism, and creatinine to renal function.

Full code, intermediate counts, sensitivity tables and references are in trace.md
(numerical outputs in analysis/out/).
grader_notes: The agent correctly performed the computational workflow: bread-spiker classification, covariate-adjusted regression, and filtering. Result reporting is incomplete relative to the full set of significant positive metabolites but the biological interpretation and source grounding are strong.

QUESTION: From lung cancer patients with matched tumor-sample microbiome and RNA-seq data,
is Kocuria significantly associated with poor prognosis?
(Univariate Cox Proportional Hazards on each microbiome taxon; "poor prognosis" = HR > 1 and p < 0.05.)

SHORT ANSWER
Yes under the literal criterion, but no in any statistically meaningful sense. Kocuria is nominally
associated with worse overall survival (HR > 1, p < 0.05), but that hit is driven by a single patient,
does not survive multiple-testing correction, and disappears under alternative but equally defensible
definitions of the variable. It should NOT be reported as a poor-prognosis marker.

ANALYSIS COHORT
- TCGA_RNA-01A.csv: 462 tumour samples x 10,508 columns; survival_time (days) and survival_status
  (1 = death, 0 = censored): 176 deaths / 286 censored, follow-up 4-6,812 days (median 582).
- TCGA_microbiota-01A.csv: 667 rows x 252 columns (250 taxa, all "investigation" = TCGA-LUAD).
  667 rows collapse to 507 unique patients (160 replicate-library rows: 116 pairs, 22 triples);
  the highest-read library per patient was kept. 20 of 250 taxa are all-zero -> 230 taxa tested.
- Matched cohort (inner join on TCGA barcode): 457 patients, 173 deaths (37.9%).
- Relative abundance was computed by total-sum scaling per sample (primary scale, expressed in %).
  Library sizes are extremely heterogeneous: 13 to 7,075,634 reads (median 81).

SCREEN RESULT (univariate Cox, all 230 taxa, relative abundance in %)
- 94/230 taxa had HR > 1.
- 17/230 taxa met the requested criterion HR > 1 and p < 0.05 (e.g. Dissoconium HR 18.7, p = 2.4e-05;
  Peptoniphilus HR 1.4e+08, p = 3.9e-05; Ustilago HR 34.8, p = 6.9e-03; Rothia HR 3.16, p = 0.014;
  Enterococcus HR 5.6e+10, p = 0.027; Kocuria HR 76.3, p = 0.0276). None had HR < 1 and p < 0.05.
- Only 2/230 taxa survive Benjamini-Hochberg FDR < 0.05 (Dissoconium q = 0.0045; Peptoniphilus
  q = 0.0045), and both have implausible effect sizes with only 16-28 positive samples.

KOCURIA RESULT
Nominal (the requested definition): Kocuria relative abundance is associated with POOR prognosis.
  HR = 76.3 per 1% relative abundance, 95% CI 1.61-3,611, Wald p = 0.0276 (R survival 3.6.4);
  independently reproduced with lifelines 0.30.3: HR = 76.31, 95% CI 1.613-3,610.9, p = 0.0276.
  Kocuria is positive in 45/457 patients (9.8%); maximum relative abundance 0.546%, median among
  positives 0.0027%. Cox z = 2.20; score/log-rank p = 0.024; likelihood-ratio p = 0.090;
  concordance 0.488 (chance level); proportional-hazards assumption satisfied (cox.zph p = 0.74).

Why the nominal result is not credible:
1. Multiple testing: BH q = 0.489 for Kocuria (nowhere near significant among 230 tests).
2. Effect size instability: 95% CI spans ~3.4 orders of magnitude (1.6 to 3,611); concordance 0.49.
3. Scale dependence: significant only for untransformed abundance; on log10(relative abundance)
   p = 0.671 and on log10(counts+1) p = 0.740. No monotone dose-response.
4. Single-patient dependence (leave-one-out, 457 refits): median p = 0.028, but omitting ONE patient
   (TCGA-05-4402-01A, Kocuria = 0.546%, the cohort maximum, 199 reads, died at 244 days) gives
   p = 0.972. Only 1 of 457 omissions crosses p = 0.05.
5. Binary definition (detected vs not detected): HR 0.972, 95% CI 0.603-1.568, p = 0.908; log-rank
   detected vs not p = 0.908; Kaplan-Meier across not-detected / lower-half / upper-half of positives
   log-rank p = 0.427 (upper half vs rest p = 0.334). No survival separation at all.
6. Screen calibration: 200 permutations of the survival labels through the identical pipeline yield a
   mean of 24.0 taxa with HR > 1 and p < 0.05 (SD 9.6, up to 58) versus 17 observed (empirical
   p = 0.78). The screen generates at least this many "poor prognosis" taxa by construction, and
   dropping each nominal hit's single most-abundant sample leaves 0/17 significant.
7. Confounding by sequencing depth/biomass: Kocuria is detected almost only in high-biomass samples
   (median 75,291 vs 66.5 total reads; Wilcoxon p = 1.9e-20), so the raw-count association is a depth
   artefact; after adjusting for log10 biomass the relative-abundance association remains only
   marginal (HR 56.8, p = 0.045) while biomass itself is not prognostic (HR 1.07, p = 0.14).
8. Preprocessing sensitivity: if the 160 replicate microbiome libraries are summed instead of
   max-selected, Kocuria HR = 35.6, p = 0.070 (not significant).

INTERPRETATION
Kocuria is a low-virulence, opportunistic Gram-positive coccus (Micrococcaceae, Actinobacteria) and
the present cohort carries it at ~0.5% or less of the tumour microbial community in only 9.8% of
patients. The positive HR is a sparse-data/outlier artefact: one patient with an unusually high
Kocuria fraction and a relatively short survival dominates the likelihood, which is the classic
separation/single-influence failure mode of univariate Cox models on zero-inflated covariates.
The broader screen is equally fragile - the entire 17-taxon "poor prognosis" list collapses when one
sample per taxon is removed.

FINAL ANSWER
Kocuria does satisfy the task's literal criterion - its univariate Cox hazard ratio is > 1 with
p < 0.05 (HR = 76.3 per 1% relative abundance, 95% CI 1.61-3,611, p = 0.0276, n = 457, 173 deaths) -
so it appears in the poor-prognosis taxa list. However, Kocuria is NOT significantly associated with
poor prognosis in any robust sense: the result is not significant after FDR correction (q = 0.49),
vanishes under log transformation (p = 0.67) and under a detected/not-detected definition
(p = 0.91; log-rank p = 0.43-0.91), is abolished by excluding a single patient (p = 0.97), is no more
common than expected under a permutation null (17 observed vs 24.0 expected hits), and is at most
marginal after adjusting for microbial biomass (p = 0.045). Conclusion: no, Kocuria should not be
considered a significant poor-prognosis marker in this matched TCGA-LUAD tumour-microbiome/RNA-seq
cohort; the nominal association is an artefact of sparse, zero-inflated taxa and one influential
sample.

LIMITATIONS
Cross-sectional relative-abundance data cannot establish causality or direction; no clinical
covariates (age, sex, stage, smoking, treatment, histology) are available in these files, so all HRs
are unadjusted - stage in particular is unmeasured and is the dominant LUAD prognostic factor; only
45/457 patients are Kocuria-positive; genus-level data with no functional or strain resolution; no
compositionality-aware model (CLR/ILR) or zero-inflated model was fitted; no independent cohort was
available for validation; and the provenance of the microbiome table could not be verified from the
files themselves.
grader_notes: The agent executed a complete and rigorous analysis, correctly constructing the matched cohort, running univariate Cox models, applying the exact poor-prognosis rule, verifying Kocuria's statistical significance under the literal criterion, and providing full reporting with well-grounded sources.

ANSWER: Can WGCNA identify modules of co-expressed genes in ALS spinal cord?

SHORT ANSWER
Yes. WGCNA on the post-mortem cervical spinal-cord RNA-seq of this cohort (16,463 expressed
genes, 168 samples: 135 ALS / 33 control, after quality filtering) yields 19 co-expression
modules plus a small grey bin (781 genes). The modules are biologically coherent (11 of 19 are
significantly enriched for a specific CNS cell type, 18 have coherent GO biological-process
programmes), 14 of 19 are differentially shifted in ALS after adjustment for age, sex, RNA
integrity and library preparation, and the module structure and the disease effect both
replicate in the lumbar and thoracic spinal cord, including in completely independent de-novo
WGCNA runs. The caveat is biological rather than statistical: in bulk post-mortem tissue most
of the ALS module signal is cell-compositional, and only a minority of modules retain an ALS
association once cell-type marker scores are covariates.

WHAT WAS DONE
- Per region: raw counts -> ALS/Control only -> filter to CPM > 1 in >= 50% of samples
  (58,884 -> 16,463 cervical, 16,545 lumbar, 16,467 thoracic genes) -> DESeq2 VST
  (blind = TRUE) -> sample-network outlier screen (connectivity Z < -2.5 removes 6 cervical,
  3 lumbar, 3 thoracic samples).
- Cervical network: signed network, biweight mid-correlation, soft-thresholding power
  beta = 18 (best scale-free fit R^2 = 0.831; no power in 1-20 reached the 0.85 target, so the
  maximum-fit power, which is also the WGCNA FAQ value for signed bicor networks with > 40
  samples, was used) -> blockwiseModules (minModuleSize 30, deepSplit 2, mergeCutHeight 0.25).
- Biology: Fisher enrichment of the 8 x 100 Mathys et al. 2019 single-nucleus marker sets,
  clusterProfiler GO-BP enrichment, curated ALS-gene overlay.
- Disease association: module-trait correlations (BH-FDR over 247 module-trait pairs) plus
  limma linear models with covariates; gene-level limma DE; per-module gene-level t statistics.
- Composition control: 8 cell-type marker scores (mean z-scored marker expression) tested for
  ALS vs control, then added as covariates to the module model.
- Replication: (a) cervical module labels projected into lumbar/thoracic eigengenes,
  WGCNA modulePreservation (50 permutations); (b) independent de-novo WGCNA in each region.
- Robustness: network rebuilt at beta = 12; eigengenes recomputed with all samples.

KEY QUANTITATIVE RESULTS
1. Network/modules: 19 modules + 781 grey genes, sizes 3,950 (M1) to 92 (M19). beta = 12
   rebuild gives 17 modules with 46-96% gene overlap and module ALS effect sizes correlated
   r = 0.974 with the primary run; retaining the 6 outlier samples changes effects by < 4%.
2. Cell-type identity (Fisher OR, FDR): M5 neuronal Ex/In (29.5x / 24.1x, FDR 2.2e-50 /
   8.9e-45; "modulation of chemical synaptic transmission", FDR 1.5e-53); M10 oligodendrocyte
   (33.9x), M7 oligodendrocyte differentiation; M9 astrocyte (22.4x); M12 microglia (14.8x),
   M13 microglia (25.0x), M14 microglia (4.3x); M11 endothelial (36.3x, "angiogenesis" FDR
   4.1e-34); M17 pericyte (34.9x); M16 OPC (23.8x); M4 cytoplasmic/mitochondrial translation;
   M8/M18 oxidative phosphorylation; M19 cilium movement (FDR 2.4e-73). 18 of 19 modules have
   GO-BP terms at FDR < 0.05 (3,349 terms total).
3. ALS association (adjusted for age, sex, RIN, library prep; FDR over 19 modules): 14 of 19
   modules significant. Strongest: M12 microglial/immune UP (+0.116, FDR 9.4e-17; 94% of its
   385 genes are individually DE); M7 oligodendrocyte DOWN (-0.092, FDR 6.9e-13); M10
   oligodendrocyte DOWN (-0.094, FDR 1.2e-11); M18 electron transport DOWN (-0.074,
   FDR 1.4e-09); M14 acute inflammatory UP (+0.084); M3 ncRNA silencing DOWN (-0.076);
   M8 OXPHOS UP (+0.074); M9 astrocyte-adhesion UP (+0.067); M4 translation UP (+0.053);
   M13 microglial immunity UP (+0.057). Gene level: 9,828/16,463 genes (59.7%) at FDR < 0.05
   (4,819 up / 5,009 down). Top up: CHIT1 (+2.79), GPNMB (+2.58), LYZ (+2.02), APOC1 (+1.99),
   CTSS (+1.52), MSR1 (+1.54), APOE (+1.23) - all in the microglial module M12. Top down:
   NEFH (-1.06), PRDM2, ABTB2, STMN2 (-0.58), UNC13A (-0.70), MBP (-0.74), PLP1 (-0.42).
4. Cell composition: ALS cord shows higher microglial (+0.220, FDR 1.2e-05) and astrocytic
   (+0.128, FDR 1.6e-05) marker scores and lower oligodendrocyte (-0.237, FDR 7.6e-13) and
   (nominally) excitatory-neuron (-0.104, FDR 0.081) scores. Adding the 8 cell-type scores as
   covariates removes the ALS association from 11 of the 14 modules (median attenuation 94.8%).
   Three modules survive: M12 microglial (+0.026, FDR 0.014), M4 cytoplasmic translation
   (+0.047, FDR 0.014, only 12% attenuation), and M6 mRNA destabilisation (significant only
   after adjustment, -0.044, FDR 0.014).
5. Replication across spinal-cord levels: module ALS effect sizes correlate r = 0.944
   (cervical vs lumbar; 19/19 modules same sign) and r = 0.870 (cervical vs thoracic; 16/19).
   modulePreservation Zsummary > 10 for all 19 modules in both other regions (19.1-72.1 in
   lumbar, 25.5-79.1 in thoracic = strong preservation). Independent de-novo WGCNA: lumbar
   21 modules, 13 ALS-associated;
   thoracic 37 modules, 6 ALS-associated - in both, oligodendrocyte modules go down and
   microglial/astrocyte modules go up.
6. ALS genetics aligns with the modules: M12 contains CHIT1, GPNMB, GRN; the down-regulated
   neuronal M5 contains UNC13A, STMN2, KIF5A, NEFH (the TDP-43 cryptic-splicing targets);
   M1 contains TARDBP, C9orf72, TBK1, NEK1, MATR3, TMEM106B; M8 contains SOD1, OPTN, VCP.
   C9orf72 carriers show no eigengene difference from non-carriers (smallest FDR 0.091).

INTERPRETATION
Three coordinated programmes define this ALS spinal cord. (i) A microglial innate-immune
program (M12 MHC class II / immune signalling, hubs BTK, CD68, CTSS, HLA-DMA; plus M13, M14,
M15) is switched on and is the single strongest result; it is also the one module whose shift
clearly survives cell-composition adjustment, consistent with microglia both increasing in
number and shifting to an activated antigen-presenting state. (ii) A cytoplasmic/
mitochondrial translation and proteostasis program (M4) is up-regulated essentially
independently of composition. (iii) Oligodendrocyte/myelin programmes (M7, M10, M18; MBP,
PLP1, BCAS1) are switched off, matching the reduced oligodendrocyte marker score. Neuronal
modules containing the TDP-43 targets UNC13A and STMN2 move down but lose significance after
adjustment and are only partly replicated in the lumbar cord.

WHAT THE ANALYSIS CANNOT CONCLUDE
- No protein-level orthogonal validation: the Oeckl et al. proteomics dataset named in the
  task brief is not present in the workspace (only RNA-seq, GENCODE references and the Mathys
  marker object are available), so no protein claim is made.
- Bulk tissue cannot separate a cell-intrinsic expression change from a change in cell
  proportions; the marker-score adjustment is a first-order, brain-reference-based correction
  and cannot eliminate the ambiguity.
- Post-mortem end-stage, cross-sectional data cannot establish causality or temporal order;
  the glial programs may be secondary to motor-neuron loss.
- Power is limited by controls (36 cervical, 33 lumbar, 11 thoracic). Thoracic can only
  replicate large effects.
- Module boundaries are a modelling choice (beta 18 vs 12 changes membership by up to 54% for
  some modules), so module gene lists should not be treated as fixed gene sets across studies,
  even though the disease-relevant conclusions are robust (r = 0.974).
- Residual confounding by post-mortem interval, agonal state and ethnicity is possible; those
  fields are absent from the metadata.
grader_notes: The agent performed a comprehensive and rigorous WGCNA analysis with detailed preprocessing, module detection, enrichment testing, and reporting; only the ALS-only subsetting requirement was not strictly met, as controls were included for dysregulation testing.

larger background (knockdown list alone p = 2.5e-5; ~20,000-gene transcriptome approximate
background p = 1.3e-13), and the 37 genes all go up in the overexpression experiment and down in
the knockdown experiment (a perfect mirror).

Caveats
- It is a nominal result only: across all 50 MSigDB Hallmark sets on the shared list (Benjamini-
  Hochberg FDR), G2M checkpoint has FDR = 0.286, and HALLMARK_MITOTIC_SPINDLE (60/1,543,

Baseline (DMSO, 24 h) transcriptional signatures of the four GDPx2 primary cell types:
AoSMC, skeletal muscle myoblasts (SkMM), dermal fibroblasts and melanocytes.

SHORT ANSWER
The four primary cell types have clearly distinct, non-overlapping baseline signatures at
the sample level, but they share a large common mesenchymal/core transcriptome that keeps
all pairwise correlations high. The most similar pair is SKELETAL MUSCLE MYOBLASTS and
DERMAL FIBROBLASTS (pseudobulk Pearson r = 0.9225), followed by AoSMC - SkMM (r = 0.9103)
and AoSMC - fibroblasts (r = 0.8953). Melanocytes are the outlier lineage, least similar to
everything (r = 0.8577 - 0.8710).

DATA USED
Baseline was defined as the DMSO vehicle wells (sample_type = "Ginkgo Neg Control - DMSO"):
576 libraries, 144 per cell type, all at 24 h, in 8 plates per cell type, at 0.0625 / 0.1875 /
0.625 % v/v DMSO. Metadata had 17,712 rows but only 11,808 unique sample_id (5,904 ids appear
twice with byte-identical content, 5,904 once); the h5 matrix is 11,808 samples x 59,427 genes.
QC removed 3 failed
AoSMC libraries (5,383 / 6,037 / 14,311 UMI vs a median 1.37 M) leaving 573 samples, and
37 MT- genes plus 41,171 genes detected in <10 % of wells, leaving 18,219 genes. Values were
normalized as log2(CPM+1); a median-of-ratios size-factor arm gave the same conclusions.

1) DISTINCT, NOT OVERLAPPING
- PCA on 2,000 highly variable genes gives PC1 40.7 %, PC2 26.7 %, PC3 20.5 %, PC4 0.4 %:
  four non-touching clouds, one per cell type.
- Average-linkage clustering of individual wells into 4 clusters matches the cell_line label
  perfectly: ARI = 1.000 (AoSMC 141, SkMM 144, fibroblast 144, melanocyte 144).
- Silhouette width 0.713 in HVG space and 0.889 on 10 PCs; between-type / within-type
  distance ratio 3.24; leave-one-out 5-NN classification 573/573 = 100 % accurate.
- Variance decomposition: for the 1,000 most variable genes, a median 93.7 % of variance is
  between cell types and only 0.5 % between plates within a cell type, so the separation is
  biological, not a plate/library artefact.
- 17,811 / 18,219 genes (97.8 %) differ significantly across the four types
  (Kruskal-Wallis q < 0.05) and 3,289 - 5,188 genes per pair differ by >2-fold with q < 0.05.
- Each cell type has a large exclusive gene set (one-vs-rest, q<0.05, log2FC>1,
  detection-specificity>0.5): AoSMC 449, SkMM 345, fibroblasts 459, melanocytes 562 genes.
  Marker-set overlap is negligible (Jaccard <= 0.046 for all pairs).
- Split-half reproducibility of each type's pseudobulk profile is r = 0.9993 - 0.9996, so the
  platform's own noise ceiling is far above the between-type differences.

2) SIMILARITY RANKING (most to least similar)
 1. SkMM - dermal fibroblast      r = 0.9225  (95 % bootstrap CI 0.9214 - 0.9230)
 2. AoSMC - SkMM                  r = 0.9103  (0.9092 - 0.9109)
 3. AoSMC - dermal fibroblast     r = 0.8953  (0.8939 - 0.8962)
 4. fibroblast - melanocyte       r = 0.8710  (0.8697 - 0.8717)
 5. SkMM - melanocyte             r = 0.8676  (0.8660 - 0.8684)
 6. AoSMC - melanocyte            r = 0.8577  (0.8563 - 0.8585)
SkMM-fibroblast is the single most similar pair in 1,000/1,000 bootstrap replicates; the
paired difference versus the runner-up (AoSMC-SkMM) is +0.0122 (95 % CI 0.0112 - 0.0132,
P(delta>0) = 1.000). The ranking is identical under five further metrics (Spearman; 2,000
HVGs; the 0.0625 % DMSO negative-control-only subset of 48 samples per type, where silhouette
is 0.894 and ARI 1.000; median-of-ratios size-factor normalization; mean sample-level Pearson
r over all 141x144 cross-type sample pairs). Masking one cell type's exclusive markers raises
the remaining correlations (fibroblast-melanocyte 0.8710 -> 0.8970 after removing melanocyte
markers) without changing the order.

3) BIOLOGY BEHIND THE ORDERING
- SkMM and dermal fibroblasts are both mesoderm-derived, ECM-producing mesenchymal cells and
  share collagen/ECM genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, DCN, LUM, FN1, VIM); they also
  have the fewest strongly divergent genes of any pair (907 with |log2FC| > 2). AoSMC is the
  third member of this mesenchymal triad (top-1,000 gene-set Jaccard with SkMM 0.634,
  the highest of any pair).
- Melanocytes are neural-crest-derived and their baseline is dominated by the pigment
  programme: MLANA (+12.9 log2 vs the other three types), TYRP1 (+12.1), PMEL (+11.8),
  S100B (+10.4), TYR (+9.8), PLP1 (+9.7), DCT (+9.5), SOX10 (+7.8, detected in 100 % of
  melanocyte wells and 0 % elsewhere), EDNRB, GPR143.
- AoSMC baselines are dominated by an inflammatory, not a contractile, programme: IL1B
  (+10.4), CXCL6 (+9.4), IL6 (+9.2), ESM1 (+8.6), CD24 (+8.5), IL33 (+8.4), PTGS2 (+8.1),
  SFRP4 (+6.8), IL11, PTGIS. Enrichr confirms TNF-alpha signalling via NF-kB (q = 1.2e-5),
  KRAS signalling up (q = 5e-6), inflammatory response (q = 7.3e-4), regulation of
  angiogenesis (q = 0.028) and sterol homeostasis (q = 0.028). Canonical SMC contractile genes
  are low in AoSMC (ACTA2 0.67 log2 CPM, MYH11 0.09, TAGLN 4.59, MYOCD 0.13) and are highest
  in SkMM, i.e. the AoSMC cultures are in a serum-culture dedifferentiated / synthetic state.
  Fibroblasts show the expected ECM programme (extracellular structure organization,
  q = 0.033; KRAS-up, q = 4.4e-4) and SkMM show a myogenic programme (MYF5 +2.3, DES +2.2,
  MYOD1, CLEC3B, MEOX2, H19).

4) WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SCREENING PLATFORM
Baseline signatures are distinct enough that compound responses measured within one cell type
cannot be mistaken for the cell-type baseline, and no pair of types is so similar that their
compound profiles should be treated as interchangeable. The three mesenchymal types
(AoSMC, SkMM, fibroblast) form a similarity cluster in which shared mesenchymal biology will
drive correlated compound responses, and SkMM-fibroblast is the pair most likely to respond
similarly. Melanocytes provide the most orthogonal baseline in the panel.

LIMITATIONS
- Only one timepoint (24 h) and only vehicle-treated wells: "baseline" = DMSO 24 h, and there
  is no untreated reference in this cohort. The DMSO-level effect is small (pseudobulk
  correlation across the three vehicle levels r = 0.9973 - 0.9992 within a cell type; median
  variance explained by vehicle level 2.0 - 2.9 % for the most variable genes) but not zero.
- Absolute r values are not identities: the four types share most of their expressed
  transcriptome, so the informative output is the ranking, not the value (r = 0.92 still
  corresponds to 3,720 genes changing >2-fold between SkMM and fibroblasts).
- Cell-type labels are taken as given. Melanocyte, fibroblast and myoblast identities are
  independently supported by canonical markers (23/38 external markers peak in the expected
  type), but the AoSMC wells express an inflammatory rather than a contractile SMC programme,
  which this dataset alone cannot attribute to dedifferentiation versus a labelling or
  donor-state issue.
- Bulk 3'-end RNA-seq with no single-cell resolution; donor/stromal contamination cannot be
  formally excluded, although the perfect clustering argues against it.
- Pathway enrichment for SkMM and melanocyte marker sets did not reach q < 0.05 in generic
  libraries; those programme names rest on individual marker genes rather than on enrichment.
- Whether baseline similarity predicts similarity of compound responses is not tested here.
grader_notes: The agent performed a thorough analysis but deviated from the expected pipeline in several key areas: baseline subsetting, TruncatedSVD, K-means, and specific marker evidence, resulting in B-level performance on most criteria, though limitations and sourcing were strong.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-10-3: ML screening of membraneless-organelle (MLO) participants
==============================================================================

BOTTOM LINE
-----------
Yes: the published phase-separation (PS) predictors are consistently and substantially
better at screening MLO-participant datasets than at screening the membrane-bound
organelle control — but this holds firmly only for the five disorder/condensate-axis
classifiers (PdPS-10fea, SaPS-10fea, PdPS-8fea, catGRANULE, SaPS-8fea). The two classical
prion-like/composition scores (PScore, PLAAC) are at or below chance for every dataset and
show essentially no MLO-vs-control advantage.

SETUP
-----
Positives = each of six curated 0/1 datasets (primary sheet "Training proteins removed");
negatives = the fixed non-PS background hNoPS (8,801 proteins in the master table;
8,799 scored; 8,170 after removing the 629 background proteins that are themselves members
of a curated list). Human proteins only; 116,806 per-sequence scores from
sequence_prediction.xlsx; AUC (rank/Mann-Whitney) with DeLong SE; paired DeLong tests on a
shared negative pool for MLO-vs-control.

CLASSIFICATION OF THE DATASETS
------------------------------
MLO participants (4): OpenCell nuclear punctae (n=115 scored), DACT1-particulate proteome
(251), G3BP1 proximity labeling (241), PhaSepDB high-throughput (1,712).
Controls (2): Proteomics of human mitochondri (1,120, membrane-bound organelle) and
Amyloid fiber-forming proteins (62, non-MLO aggregation control).

SCREENING PERFORMANCE (AUC vs the clean hNoPS background; 0.5 = chance)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
predictor    MLO mean | PhaSepDB  DACT1  G3BP1  OpenCell || mito   amyloid
PdPS-10fea     0.801   |  0.769    0.833  0.841   0.763   || 0.564  0.605
SaPS-10fea     0.738   |  0.688    0.773  0.818   0.672   || 0.490  0.571
PdPS-8fea      0.668   |  0.679    0.666  0.634   0.692   || 0.473  0.505
catGRANULE     0.643   |  0.674    0.628  0.715   0.554   || 0.522  0.472
SaPS-8fea      0.641   |  0.652    0.630  0.630   0.652   || 0.466  0.459
PScore         0.464   |  0.516    0.399  0.425   0.517   || 0.415  0.462
PLAAC          0.443   |  0.494    0.332  0.455   0.493   || 0.426  0.410

(Background n = 8,170 for catGRANULE/SaPS/PdPS, 8,144 for PLAAC, 7,421 for PScore.)
Union of the four MLO lists (n=2,047): PdPS-10fea 0.771 [0.760-0.782], SaPS-10fea 0.694,
PdPS-8fea 0.668, catGRANULE 0.663, SaPS-8fea 0.641, PScore 0.501, PLAAC 0.482.

MLO vs CONTROL — STATISTICAL TEST
---------------------------------
56 paired DeLong comparisons (4 MLO datasets x 2 controls x 7 predictors):
  * 51/56 (91%) have a higher AUC on the MLO dataset;
  * 43/56 are significant (p<0.05) in favour of the MLO dataset;
  * exactly 1/56 is significant the other way: PLAAC, DACT1-particulate proteome (0.332)
    vs mitochondria (0.426), delta = -0.094, z = -4.85, p = 4.6e-06.
  * mean AUC gaps (MLO mean minus control): PdPS-10fea +0.237/+0.196,
    SaPS-10fea +0.248/+0.166, PdPS-8fea +0.195/+0.163, catGRANULE +0.121/+0.171,
    SaPS-8fea +0.176/+0.182 (vs mitochondria / vs amyloid), but only PScore +0.050/+0.003
    and PLAAC +0.017/+0.033.
  * each of the five condensate-axis classifiers ranks all 4 MLO sets above BOTH controls
    (20/20 of those comparisons); PScore and PLAAC do so in only 2-3 of 4 MLO sets.

OPERATIONAL SCREEN (recall at a 5% false-positive budget on the background)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
PdPS-10fea recovers 36.5% of G3BP1, 31.5% of DACT1, 29.6% of OpenCell and 27.2% of
PhaSepDB members (5.4-7.3x over the 5% random expectation) vs only 5.0% of mitochondrial
and 8.1% of amyloid members. Using the top 5% of the whole human proteome as the threshold
(no dependence on the hand-built background) gives the same ordering: 23.7%/18.7%/21.7%/
16.4% for the four MLO sets vs 1.8% (mitochondria) and 8.1% (amyloid).

PREDICTOR RANKING (stable across datasets)
------------------------------------------
PdPS-10fea (best in all 6 datasets) > SaPS-10fea > PdPS-8fea > catGRANULE (most
dataset-dependent: 0.715 on G3BP1, 0.554 on OpenCell) > SaPS-8fea >> PScore > PLAAC.
The 10-feature SaPS/PdPS hybrids beat their 8-feature forms; Spearman rho between predictors
on the background is 0.80 (SaPS-8fea vs PdPS-8fea) and 0.77 (PdPS-8fea vs PdPS-10fea), so
the top ranks are not seven independent measurements.

DATASET RANKING
---------------
G3BP1 (0.841) > DACT1 (0.833) > PhaSepDB (0.769) ~ OpenCell (0.763) >> mitochondria (0.564)
> amyloid (0.605, best predictor). Punctae/particulate microscopy lists are the hardest to
screen; high-throughput PhaSepDB is intermediate.

WHY PScore AND PLAAC FAIL
-------------------------
PScore is heavily discretised (94.6% duplicate values) and the hNoPS background is
PScore-high by construction (median 0.94 in background vs 0.42 for DACT1 members), so its
AUCs fall below 0.5 for DACT1 (0.399) and G3BP1 (0.425). PLAAC medians (-0.24 background,
-0.26 OpenCell, -0.34 DACT1) show the curated lists are not prion-like-domain enriched
relative to this background. The SaPS/PdPS classifiers instead separate the file's own
reference classes by ~10x in score (hSaPS median SaPS-10fea 0.928 vs hNoPS 0.071; hPdPS
median PdPS-10fea 0.923 vs hNoPS 0.108), which is what produces the high MLO AUCs.

ROBUSTNESS
----------
* Using the literal hNoPS set (including the 629 proteins that are also list members)
  changes every predictor mean AUC by <=0.006 - the contamination is immaterial.
* Using the "Original data" sheet (which still contains 28 hSaPS + 46 hPdPS PS-training
  proteins) inflates PScore/PLAAC by up to +0.055 and leaves SaPS/PdPS unchanged (+0.02);
  the primary sheet ("Training proteins removed", 0/629 PS-flag overlap) is the
  conservative choice and the ranking is identical under both.
* Under both background variants and under a background-free proteome-wide screen the
  ordering and the MLO-versus-control gap are unchanged.

INTERPRETATION
--------------
MLO participants carry the low-complexity/aromatic-charge-RNA-binding determinants that the
SaPS/PdPS-style classifiers read; membrane-bound organelle proteins are localised by
hydrophobic transmembrane and signal sequences instead, and their score distributions are
indistinguishable from the non-PS background (mitochondrial median SaPS-10fea 0.071 = hNoPS
0.071). Amyloid-fibre proteins, which aggregate but do not form physiological condensates,
also fail to separate (best AUC 0.605), i.e. these classifiers capture condensate-specific
composition rather than generic aggregation propensity.

LIMITATIONS
-----------
The hNoPS background is annotation-derived, not random, so the PScore/PLAAC results partly
measure that selection. List membership is enrichment (proximity labelling, punctae imaging,
co-fractionation), not demonstrated self-assembly. The six lists overlap (PhaSepDB ∩ G3BP1 =
128 accessions), so the 56 DeLong tests are dependent and not FDR-controlled - the 43/56
figure is a consistency statistic, not 43 independent discoveries. Dataset sizes range from
62 to 1,712, so the amyloid and OpenCell CIs span +/-0.06-0.09 AUC. PhaSepDB has zero overlap
with the human master table and 620 list accessions could not be scored at all, so its
results rest on 1,712/2,415 entries (71%). The SaPS/PdPS feature definitions are not
distributed with the data, so the source of their advantage cannot be attributed to specific
features here.

ARTEFACTS
---------
analysis/auc_table.csv (primary results), analysis/delong_mlo_vs_control.csv (56 paired
tests), analysis/aggregate_auc.csv, analysis/predictor_ranking.csv,
analysis/predictor_spearman.csv, analysis/auc_union_mlo.csv, analysis/proteome_screening.csv,
analysis/background_variants.csv, analysis/auc_table_contaminated_background.csv,
analysis/auc_table_original_list.csv, analysis/dataset_overlap.csv,
analysis/class_composition.csv, analysis/auc_master_subset.csv, analysis/disorder_features.csv,
analysis/figure_auc_heatmap.png. Full methods and code: trace.md.
grader_notes: The analysis is rigorous, correctly identifies and constructs the evaluation, appropriately handles missing data, and provides statistically grounded MLO-vs-control comparison with source traceability.

DA-20-4 — Does dabrafenib show consistent or divergent transcriptional responses across the
four primary human cell types (aortic smooth-muscle cells / AoSMC, skeletal-muscle myoblasts
/ SkMM, dermal fibroblasts, melanocytes)?

SHORT ANSWER
Both — in a structured way. Dabrafenib produces a small, reproducible, shared "core" response
(a stress/mitochondrial-ATF4 program switched on, mitotic/cell-cycle programs switched off,
and ERK-pathway output genes switched on at low doses) that is present in all four cell types,
embedded in a much larger, cell-type-restricted periphery that accounts for roughly two thirds
of all differentially expressed genes. Response magnitude and dose-sensitivity differ strongly
between cell types, and five Hallmark programs that are statistically significant in all four
cell types move in OPPOSITE directions in one cell type. Dabrafenib is nevertheless one of the
more concordant compounds of its own 86-compound library (rank 19/86), so "divergent" here
means "partially shared with a large tissue-specific overlay", not "unrelated responses".

EVIDENCE (data: GDPx2 Drug-seq; 1,344 samples = 768 dabrafenib + 576 DMSO vehicle, 16,574
filtered genes; limma-voom per cell type, design ~0 + treatment x dose + sequencing container,
each dose contrasted against its %DMSO-matched vehicle; DEG = FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0.5;
120/1,344 samples removed as outliers by the dataset's own utils.R rule, 1,224 analysed.)

1) MAGNITUDE IS DIVERGENT AND DOSE-DEPENDENT
Number of DEGs at each concentration (nM):

  cell type      9.5   28.5    95    300    900   3000
  AoSMC           37    191    825   2727   2991    779
  SkMM            31     77    118    958   1779   1232
  fibroblast      24    160    355    777   1689   1225
  melanocyte       0      5     47    316    617   1271

At the shared dose of 900 nM the response size differs about 5-fold (AoSMC 2,991 vs melanocyte
617); at 300 nM about 8-fold (2,727 vs 316). AoSMC is the most responsive cell type at every
dose up to 900 nM; melanocytes are the least responsive and only become the most responsive at
the highest dose (3,000 nM), where the melanocyte response is dominated by gene repression
(340 up vs 931 down) and its ERK-output genes collapse (EGR1 -1.39, JUN -1.76, ETV1 -1.01).

2) GENE-SET OVERLAP: A SMALL SHARED CORE
At 900 nM, 4,791 genes are differentially expressed in at least one cell type. Sharing:
  1 cell type  3,233 genes (67.5%)
  2 cell types   991 genes (20.7%)
  3 cell types   407 genes ( 8.5%)
  4 cell types   160 genes ( 3.3%)
The 4/4 overlap is 132x the random expectation (1.2 genes, permutation test, p <= 1e-4) and the
3/4 overlap 7.0x; the single-cell-type count is BELOW its random expectation (3,233 vs 5,164).
So the shared core is real and highly non-random, but it is a minority of the response.
Pairwise Jaccard indices are 0.088 (AoSMC-melanocyte) to 0.235 (AoSMC-SkMM), all 1.8-4.5x the
random expectation.

3) WHERE GENES ARE SHARED, DIRECTION AGREES
Among genes significant in both members of a pair, 93.2-97.9% move in the same direction; 157 of
the 160 shared-core genes agree in sign in all four cell types. Divergence is therefore mainly
"which genes respond, and how strongly", not "opposite regulation of the same gene".
Genome-wide log2FC agreement is modest and dose-dependent: pairwise Pearson r = 0.31-0.55 across
all 16,574 genes (0.39-0.61 on the DEG core) at 900 nM, versus a split-half reproducibility of the
same cell type's response of 0.87 (AoSMC), 0.81 (fibroblast), 0.79 (SkMM), 0.60 (melanocyte).
After correcting for this measurement noise, the shared component is r = 0.37-0.62
(AoSMC-SkMM 0.62 > SkMM-fibroblast 0.58 > AoSMC-fibroblast 0.52 > fibroblast-melanocyte 0.40 >
SkMM-melanocyte 0.39 > AoSMC-melanocyte 0.37). A vehicle-only (DMSO vs DMSO) cross-cell-type
baseline is centred on zero (mean r = 0.002, SD 0.18, n = 54), so the agreement is not a batch
artefact.

4) WHAT IS CONSISTENT ACROSS THE FOUR CELL TYPES
 a. A strong ATF4 / integrated-stress-response program is induced in all four cell types and is
    the single largest shared signal: mean log2FC +2.24 (AoSMC), +2.07 (SkMM), +1.91
    (fibroblast), +1.22 (melanocyte) at 900 nM; 16/16 signature genes individually significant in
    AoSMC, 15/16 in SkMM and fibroblasts and 12/16 in melanocytes. Shared-core up-genes include CHAC1, TRIB3, DDIT3 (CHOP),
    ATF4, ASNS, PSAT1, PHGDH, PSPH, SHMT2, MTHFD2, SESN2, GDF15, SLC7A11, SLC1A5, SLC38A1,
    SLC6A9, NUPR1, PCK2, CTH, CEBPB, CEBPG, EIF4EBP1, NIBAN1, ADM2 (71 genes up in all four).
    The parallel induction of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (CARS1, GARS1, IARS1, MARS1, SARS1,
    TARS1, WARS1, YARS1; KEGG aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis FDR 5e-6 on the core) is the
    transcriptional signature of amino-acid limitation.
 b. Mitotic / cell-cycle programs are repressed in all four cell types: 86 shared-core genes are
    down in 4/4, including CDK1, CCNB1, CDC20, UBE2C, RRM2, AURKA/B, PLK1, BIRC5, TPX2, ANLN,
    DLGAP5 and the centromere/kinetochore genes CENPA, CENPE, CENPK, CENPM, CENPU, CENPW;
    mitotic signature mean log2FC -1.87 (AoSMC),
    -1.85 (fibroblast), -0.97 (SkMM), -0.51 (melanocyte); HALLMARK E2F_TARGETS, G2M_CHECKPOINT
    and MITOTIC_SPINDLE are negative in all four (NES -1.4 to -2.9); ORA of the shared core is
    dominated by "sister chromatid segregation" (27/144, FDR 9.7e-17).
 c. ERK/MAPK-pathway output goes UP (not down) in every cell type at sub-cytotoxic doses:
    DUSP6 and SPRY2 (canonical ERK-output/negative-feedback genes) rise from 9.5-28.5 nM in all
    four (DUSP6 log2FC at 9.5 nM: SkMM +0.70, fibroblast +0.23, AoSMC +0.16, melanocyte +0.07),
    and HALLMARK_UNFOLDED_PROTEIN_RESPONSE, MTORC1_SIGNALING and P53_PATHWAY are up in all four
    at 900 nM. An upward ERK-output signature together with reduced proliferation in
    BRAF-wild-type cells is the transcriptional fingerprint of paradoxical (dimer-mediated) RAF
    activation rather than of plain pathway blockade.
 d. Lineage identity is retained: the melanocyte pigment program (MITF, TYR, TYRP1, DCT, PMEL,
    MLANA, SOX10) is essentially unchanged in melanocytes (mean log2FC +0.02), so the response is
    a stress/arrest overlay, not a loss of cell identity.

5) WHAT IS DIVERGENT
 a. Direction flips among programs significant in all four cell types at 900 nM: SkMM is the
    outlier for EMT (SkMM +1.66 vs -1.80/-1.92/-2.10), hypoxia (SkMM +1.49 vs -1.46 to -1.98)
    and glycolysis (SkMM +1.43 vs -1.45 to -1.85), while melanocytes are the outlier for MYC
    targets (melanocyte +2.12 vs -1.56 to -1.69) and KRAS signalling (-1.38 vs +1.61/+2.21/+1.84).
 b. Cell-type-restricted biology, not noise: SkMM-specific loss of the myogenic/contractile
    program (LMOD1 -2.47, ANKRD2 -2.01, FHL5 -2.00, HSPB7 -1.89, FABP4 -1.86, DES -1.08,
    ACTA2 -1.45); AoSMC-specific repression of MAPK-feedback/immediate-early genes (SPRY1 -2.33,
    DUSP2 -1.44, PTPRR -1.24) with the deepest mitotic collapse (UBE2C -3.13, CDC20 -3.10); a
    fibroblast-specific cytokine/ECM program (S100P +3.72, IL1RL1 +3.96, CXCL8 +1.73, IL11 +1.11,
    IL6 +0.61, COL1A1 -1.40; KEGG cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction FDR 1.7e-3; GO calcium-
    mediated signalling, cell chemotaxis, Notch signalling restricted to fibroblasts); and a
    223-gene melanocyte-restricted set (JUN, DUSP5, ISG15, ISG20, KITLG, APCDD1).
 c. Scale check: at 900 nM dabrafenib's mean cross-cell-type correlation (4-replicate profiles,
    like-for-like) is 0.233 versus a median of 0.064 for the other 85 library compounds —
    rank 19 of 86 (top 22%), i.e. above the library norm but far from interchangeable. Agreement
    between two different cell types treated with dabrafenib (0.31-0.55 raw) is also higher than
    agreement between dabrafenib and a different drug in the same cell type (median 0.119).

INTERPRETATION FOR TISSUE-SPECIFIC SAFETY AND EFFICACY
- The conserved core (ATF4/ISR induction + mitotic shutdown + low-dose ERK-output rise) is the
  part of the response that cannot be made tumour-selective and is the best candidate mediator
  of class-wide, non-tumour-restricted effects; it is present even in the two muscle cell types
  that are the dose-limiting tissues for RAF-inhibitor tolerability.
- The divergent periphery is the tissue-specific liability map: dermal fibroblasts (cytokine/
  IL-6/IL-11/CXCL8 induction with collagen repression) suggest skin inflammation/ECM remodelling
  risk; SkMM (loss of myogenic-contractile genes) suggests myotoxicity risk; AoSMC shows the
  largest and earliest transcriptional disturbance (peak 2,991 DEGs at 900 nM; GDF15 +3.70,
  TRIB3 +3.72) and is the tissue where the least selectivity is expected.
- Melanocytes — the lineage in which efficacy is sought — are transcriptionally the LEAST
  responsive at clinically attainable low-to-mid concentrations and only reach their largest
  response at 3,000 nM, where the other three cell types are already saturated or past their peak
  (AoSMC). Read strictly, this argues for a narrow transcriptional therapeutic window and against
  assuming that the melanocyte lineage is preferentially targeted at these exposures.

WHAT THIS ANALYSIS CANNOT CONCLUDE
- One donor per cell type and a single 24 h timepoint: cell type is confounded with donor,
  genotype and sequencing batch (two cell types per container set), so results describe these
  four primary isolates, not the four tissues; inter-individual variability is not estimable.
- Transcriptional consistency is not functional consistency: no viability, apoptosis, phospho-ERK
  or histology data are present, and BRAF/NRAS/RAS genotype of the isolates is not given, so
  mutation-selective pharmacology cannot be tested.
- A 24 h snapshot cannot separate direct drug effects from secondary consequences (e.g. whether
  the ISR is a primary response or downstream of stress/arrest); the paradoxical-activation
  reading of the upward ERK-output genes is an inference from pattern, not a measurement.
- Melanocytes have the poorest assay quality (median sequencing saturation 0.28 vs 0.59;
  mitochondrial reads 15.8% vs 5.3%; split-half reliability 0.60 vs 0.79-0.87), so part of their
  small response and apparent divergence is likely measurement noise; noise corrections only
  apply on average.
- Dabrafenib has 8x more replicates than any other library compound, so the rank 19/86 statement
  holds for equal-depth comparison only.
- The AoSMC 300-vs-900 nM peak location is not robust to the outlier heuristic (2,727 vs 4,686
  DEGs at 300 nM with/without outlier removal); the cell-type ranking is robust, the peak
  location should not be over-interpreted.

BOTTOM LINE
Dabrafenib's response across AoSMC, SkMM, dermal fibroblasts and melanocytes is largely divergent
in composition and magnitude (two thirds of responsive genes are significant in only one cell
type; 5-8-fold differences in DEG counts; effect-size correlations of only r = 0.31-0.55, i.e.
0.37-0.62 after noise correction) but not in an unstructured way: it is anchored on a
reproducible shared core, an ATF4/integrated-stress induction plus mitotic repression plus
low-dose ERK-output activation, that is concordant in ALL FOUR cell types and accounts for every
programme that moves in identical directions. Tissue-specific safety assessment should therefore
treat the shared core as class-level risk and the divergent periphery (SkMM myogenic, fibroblast
cytokine/ECM, AoSMC global amplitude, melanocyte late/shifted response) as the tissue-specific
risk, rather than expecting one uniform response.
grader_notes: The work is rigorous in general QC, DE, and GSEA but deviates from the specific rubric requirements by omitting effect-size shrinkage and ranking GSEA by moderated t rather than shrunken log2FC, and it does not provide the expected cell-type-specific interpretations for KRAS, EMT, and melanocyte pathways; source reliability is strong.

DA-4-6 — Proportion of non-MPR patients with high Texp levels and favourable RFS

ANSWER
------
Among the 70 non-MPR patients in the cohort, 26 have high Texp cell levels that predict
favourable recurrence-free survival despite the absence of pathological response:

    * 26 / 70 = 37.1% of all non-MPR patients
    * 26 / 64 = 40.6% of non-MPR patients with evaluable TCR data
      (6 non-MPR patients have no Texp.in.Tex.relevant*10 value)

So the answer is approximately 37-41% (best single estimate 40.6% of evaluable non-MPR
patients, i.e. ~4 in 10 non-MPR patients).

DEFINITIONS USED
----------------
* non-MPR = patients without major pathological response (MPR == 'non-MPR', n = 70;
  the responder comparator is MPR + pCR, n = 89).
* "Texp cell levels" = `Texp.in.Tex.relevant*10`, the fraction of the Tex-relevant
  (tumour-antigen-reactive) CD8 compartment occupied by Texp cells. This was the only one of
  the five TCR/Texp features in the table that carried RFS information (median-split log-rank
  p = 0.0055 in the whole cohort, p = 0.00039 in non-MPR); the clone-count features
  (`numberTexClone*0.1`, `numberTregClone*0.1`, `number.of.cells.top.3.tex.clones`,
  `number.of.cells.top.3.treg.clones`) were all null (p = 0.18-0.96).
* "High" = Texp.in.Tex.relevant*10 >= the cohort median of 8.37 (median of the 138 evaluable
  patients; a pre-specifiable cut-point, not a data-optimal one).

EVIDENCE THAT THE HIGH-Texp SUBGROUP IS FAVOURABLE
--------------------------------------------------
* Recurrences: 4/26 (15.4%) in non-MPR Texp-high vs 17/38 (44.7%) in non-MPR Texp-low.
* Log-rank test, non-MPR Texp-high vs Texp-low: p = 0.011.
* Cox HR = 0.27 (95% CI 0.09-0.80, p = 0.018); adjusted for stage, histology and adjuvant
  immune-checkpoint therapy HR = 0.26 (95% CI 0.08-0.78, p = 0.017).
* Kaplan-Meier RFS at 24 months: 83.6% (non-MPR Texp-high) vs 50.1% (non-MPR Texp-low) vs
  88.6% (MPR/pCR responders).
* Non-MPR Texp-high patients are statistically indistinguishable from patients who achieved
  MPR/pCR (log-rank p = 0.41), whereas non-MPR Texp-low patients are clearly worse than
  responders (p = 6.8e-7).

THRESHOLD DEPENDENCE (sensitivity)
----------------------------------
The proportion depends on the cut-point, and the RFS advantage is preserved across all
pre-specifiable thresholds (HR 0.14-0.33):
    cohort 75th percentile (8.88)          -> 14/70 = 20.0%
    responder (MPR/pCR) median (8.53)      -> 23/70 = 32.9%
    cohort median (8.37)  [primary]        -> 26/70 = 37.1%
    cohort mean (8.13)                     -> 29/70 = 41.4%
    non-MPR median (8.05)                  -> 32/70 = 45.7%
    cohort 25th percentile (7.59)          -> 39/70 = 55.7%
    data-optimal cut-point (6.73, optimistic; not used as the answer) -> 52/70 = 74.3%
A reasonable summary range is therefore one-third to one-half of non-MPR patients, with 26/70
(37.1%) / 26/64 (40.6%) from the pre-specified median split as the headline figure.

CAVEATS
-------
The subgroup is defined and tested on the same 22 non-MPR recurrence events (4 events in the
Texp-high subgroup), median follow-up is 20.9 months, and the formal Texp x response
interaction is not significant (p = 0.26). The finding is therefore hypothesis-generating
(prognostic association within this cohort), not a validated predictive biomarker, and requires
independent validation.
grader_notes: The agent performs rigorous data handling, survival analysis, and source attribution, but it misses two rubric-specific requirements: within-non-MPR median stratification and overall 3-group log-rank / Cox contrasts against MPR.

ANSWER: Does AI-10-49 treatment lead to global changes in chromatin accessibility in
inv(16) AML (ME-1) cells?

YES, but the change is a modest GLOBAL CONTRACTION of the accessible landscape rather
than a global reorganisation: after AI-10-49 the cells have ~20-23% fewer accessible
regions, a ~19% smaller accessible footprint, about 3x more regions lost than gained,
less accessibility on every chromosome, and ~28% lower depth-normalized signal at the
regions that remain accessible. Most of the landscape is retained (about half of all
consensus regions, and 88-95% of replicate-supported regions), so the changes are
quantitative and genome-wide, not a wholesale remodelling of which regions are open.

Evidence (MACS2 ATAC-seq peak calls, GSE101790; 2 DMSO vs 2 AI-10-49 libraries;
filtered to 24 canonical hg19 chromosomes and outside the ENCODE hg19 blacklist v2):

1. Fewer accessible regions.
   66,345 (DMSO rep1), 64,248 (DMSO rep2) vs 48,105 (AI rep1), 52,486 (AI rep2) peaks
   after filtering (233,842 raw -> 231,184 filtered; 258 non-canonical contig peaks and
   2,400 blacklisted peaks removed). Mean 65,296.5 -> 50,295.5 peaks, i.e. -22.96%.
   Even normalised for depth (peaks per million nucleosome-free fragments: 26,325/26,167
   vs 11,630/11,938; mean ratio 0.449) and in a matched-N comparison (top 48,105 peaks
   per library), the treated libraries do not exceed the controls.

2. Smaller accessible footprint.
   Mean bp in peaks 8,391,466 (DMSO) -> 7,288,598 (AI-10-49), i.e. 0.293% -> 0.254% of
   the 2.86 Gb genome (ratio 0.869). Replicate-union footprint (the standard ATAC
   consensus): 11,868,909 bp -> 9,569,847 bp, ratio 0.806.

3. Losses strongly outnumber gains.
   On a common set of 101,986 union (consensus) regions: 38,785 DMSO-only ("lost",
   3.49 Mb), 13,028 AI-10-49-only ("gained", 1.20 Mb), 50,173 shared (9.75 Mb).
   Lost:gained = 2.98:1 (exact binomial p < 1e-300; Fisher OR 2.98). Restricting to
   regions supported by 2/2 replicates in their own condition (the conservative version):
   11,718 lost vs 7,825 gained = 1.50:1 (binomial p = 1.04e-171; Fisher exact p = 1.34e-128).
   Cross-recovery is asymmetric: 94.6% of AI-10-49
   replicate-supported regions are recovered by DMSO, but only 88.2% of DMSO
   replicate-supported regions are recovered by AI-10-49 (Fisher p = 1.4e-220).

4. Lower signal at retained regions.
   At the 28,461 regions detected by 2/2 replicates in all four libraries, the
   depth-normalized summit signal (MACS2 pileup column / library size in millions of
   fragments) falls from a median 3.415 to 2.460 fragments per million; median
   log2(AI-10-49/DMSO) = -0.44, with 83.6% of regions lower in the treated condition
   (Wilcoxon p < 1e-15). 10.5% of regions lose more than 2-fold; only 0.08% gain more
   than 2-fold. Note that the internally normalized narrowPeak fold-enrichment is
   HIGHER in the treated samples (median 6.8-6.9 vs 5.2-5.4), which is the expected
   signature of deeper libraries, not of accessibility - it cannot be used as a
   cross-condition signal measure.

5. The reduction is genome-wide, not locus-specific.
   The AI-10-49/DMSO peak-count ratio is below 1 on all 23 canonical chromosomes
   (chr1-22, X): median 0.757, range 0.710 (chr13) to 0.968 (chr19), Wilcoxon signed-rank
   p = 2.70e-05. No single chromosome, amplicon or inspected locus reverses the pattern:
   the MYC 500-kb window has fewer peaks after treatment (27/32 vs 20/19), and the MYC
   promoter is retained with 2/2 replicate support in both conditions in all three union
   regions (chr8:128,746,311-128,746,495; chr8:128,747,428-128,747,695; chr8:128,748,373-
   128,748,562); the 8q24 enhancer window (chr8:130.59-130.72 Mb) is unchanged (10-12
   peaks per library).

6. It is a contraction, not a reorganisation.
   49.2% of consensus regions are shared (9.75 of 14.44 Mb); 52.9% of regions are called
   in only one of four libraries, and those are weak: 67.2% of lost regions have
   narrowPeak fold enrichment < 4 (median 3.74) versus 1.1% of shared regions, and no
   region above fold 15 is condition-specific. Cross-detection at matched own-strength is
   near-symmetric (e.g. 67.4% vs 70.5% at fold 5-6). Region-level Jaccard concordance is
   0.452 within DMSO and 0.574 within AI-10-49, versus 0.464-0.497 between conditions, and
   per-region signal correlates 0.64-0.71 across conditions (0.66-0.75 within condition),
   i.e. the shape of the landscape is preserved.

7. Supporting mechanistic check (RUNX1 motif).
   Lost regions are not selectively RUNX1-bound: 1.62 RUNX1-core motifs/kb
   (TGTGGT/ACCACA) versus 1.25 in retained regions (Poisson p = 0.011), but a logistic
   model adjusting for GC content and region length gives no class effect (lost OR 1.15,
   p = 0.32; gained OR 0.82, p = 0.17). Consistent with a cell-state-level contraction
   (AI-10-49 induces apoptosis in inv(16) cells) rather than a direct, uniform loss of
   RUNX1 occupancy.

MAIN CAVEAT / LIMITATION:
The two AI-10-49 libraries contain 1.715x more nucleosome-free fragments than the two
DMSO libraries (4,136,297 and 4,396,480 vs 2,520,192 and 2,455,294), so they had more
statistical power to call peaks. The observed deficit runs OPPOSITE to that depth
advantage (a deeper condition calling ~23% fewer peaks, and recovering the other
condition's regions less well), which is why the reduction is judged real, but the
magnitude cannot be separated cleanly from a possible global library-efficiency
difference between the batches, and with only peak calls available (no BAMs/read counts;
fastq_r1_exists = False for all 16 samples) no equal-depth downsampling or count-based
differential test is possible. The ~20-23% figures should therefore be read as an upper
bound on the biological effect. The direction, the genome-wide consistency, the 1.5-3:1
loss:gain asymmetry and the reduced signal at retained regions are the robust findings.
grader_notes: The agent robustly identified the correct ATAC samples, used available peak data to quantify directional and global accessibility changes, and drew a well-supported conclusion of global chromatin contraction; the main analytical gap is lack of true per-region read-coverage quantification from BAMs, making criterion 2 partial.

HLA-DRA (+0.03) and CD14 (+0.12, FDR 0.077) are not significantly changed; LYZ is
unchanged (+0.05, FDR 0.52) — i.e. this is a state change, not a loss of monocyte identity.
Alarmins: S100A9 +0.48 (1.6e-16), S100A8 +0.25 (1.4e-3), MNDA +0.37, FCN1 +0.35, CD68 +0.34,
CCR2 +0.57 (2.6e-7), CSF1R +0.16.
71 genes reach at least 2-fold up-regulation at FDR < 0.05; 24 of the 25 ISGs are among them.

TOP DOWN-REGULATED GENES (log2 fold change, FDR)
CHD1-DT -1.28 / 4.9e-24; CA11 -0.91 / 1.1e-20; KIF22 -0.72 / 3.7e-20; SH3D19 -1.53 / 2.6e-19;
CAMK4 -1.00 / 6.8e-19; STMN3 -0.74 / 1.9e-18; HNRNPL -0.43 / 6.7e-18; CD7 -0.62 / 8.1e-18;
BIRC2 -0.43 / 2.5e-17; IL7R -0.79 / 3.2e-17; LRRC75A, SOX4, CNFN, GNLY, TC2N, PDE7B, CCR7,
LEF1, KRT10, FCMR, CD3E, LCK, TXK, MS4A1, LTB (all FDR <= 1.2e-16); FCER1A -1.08 / 8.6e-9.
Only 10 genes reach 2-fold down (CHD1-DT, SH3D19, CAMK4, PDE7B, LINC00910, EGR3, FCER1A,
ENSG00000270103, SNORD3B-2, HSPA1B) versus 71 up — the signature is asymmetric and skewed
towards induction, not repression.

BIOLOGICAL / CLINICAL INTERPRETATION
The upregulated module is a self-amplifying IFN-I circuit: master amplifier IRF7 plus
STAT1/STAT2/IRF9 and the cytosolic RNA/DNA sensors (IFIH1, IFI16, AIM2, RIGI) are induced
together with IFN effector genes (OAS1/2/3, MX1/2, IFIT1/2/3, ISG15, RSAD2, USP18, IFI6,
IFI27) and with the negative-feedback/decoy genes SIGLEC1 and USP18. Fcgamma receptors
(CD64, CD16), MHC class I (HLA-A/B/C, B2M) and the alarmins S100A8/A9 are co-induced,
consistent with an activated, immune-complex-uptaking, antigen-presenting monocyte.
The chemokine CXCL10 links the monocyte state to CXCR3+ T-cell recruitment, and the
metallothioneins (MT1E, MT2A) extend the response module.
Clinical/therapeutic reading: (i) the monocyte IFN score is a strong patient-stratification
biomarker (AUC 0.884; 64.8% of patients above the control-based threshold) and a plausible
pharmacodynamic readout; (ii) the identified axis is druggable at the receptor level
(anifrolumab, anti-IFNAR1) and downstream (JAK inhibition, e.g. baricitinib), with
SIGLEC1/CD169 already used as a monocyte-based IFN activity biomarker; (iii) individual
candidate targets/roadmap genes from this analysis are EPSTI1 (top-ranked), SIGLEC1,
CXCL10, FCGR1A/FCGR3A (Fc-mediated uptake) and the ISG15/USP18 feedback pair, while USP18
induction is best interpreted as a homeostatic brake. Treatment implications are
hypothesis-generating only: this is a cross-sectional observational dataset.

CROSS-CHECKS AND ROBUSTNESS
- DESeq2 with the identical design: 5,032 DEGs, log2FC Spearman rho = 0.998 vs edgeR;
  4,477 genes significant in edgeR + DESeq2 + donor-level Wilcoxon simultaneously.
- Unadjusted edgeR: 5,219 DEGs; adding Processing_Cohort: 2,997 DEGs; 2,650 DEGs significant
  in all five models. Direction and top ranks are unchanged in every model.
- Female-only donors (244): 4,678 of the 4,679 primary DEGs remain significant (rho = 0.936).
- Cohort-1-excluded donors (222): 4,677 of 4,678 remain; all 25 ISGs remain (rho = 0.909).
- Median-centred expression (removing any global library-composition shift): leading genes
  unchanged (EPSTI1 rank 1), mean log2FC = +0.009, i.e. no global shift artefact.
- Cell-level Wilcoxon on 10,000 + 10,000 monocytes gives the same gene ordering (top:
  ISG15, IFI6, IFI44L, LY6E, IFITM3, B2M, MT2A), but declares all 8,888 genes significant;
  it is treated only as an ordering check because cells are pseudoreplicates.
- Monocyte identity verified by markers in the compartment: S100A9 logCPM 14.3, LYZ 13.5,
  CD14 9.4, FCGR1A 6.4, FCGR3A 5.8; lymphocyte markers near background (CD3D 5.4,
  CD79A 3.9). Non-classical monocyte fraction does not differ (13.8% vs 14.9%, P = 0.17).

LIMITATIONS / WHAT THIS CANNOT SHOW
- Association, not causation: no genotype, SLEDAI, treatment dose or longitudinal data.
- Disease-state (flare/treated vs managed) is fully confounded with processing cohort 3
  (n = 11 / 6), so flare-vs-managed differences are uninterpretable; the ISG score does not
  differ between flare and managed (P = 0.29), but power is low.
- The down-regulated list is partly a composition/ambient-RNA effect: 12 of the top 100 down
  genes are canonical lymphocyte transcripts (IL7R, GNLY, CCR7, LEF1, FCMR, CD3E, CTSW, LCK,
  TXK, MS4A1, LTB, CD3D) and the per-donor T/NK transcript score is lower in SLE
  (P = 3.3e-16). A real intrinsic loss of these genes in monocytes cannot be claimed.
- Only genes detected in >= 20% of donors (8,885 of 30,172) were testable, and 10x 3' v2
  chemistry limits detection of low-expressed transcripts; the count of 4,679 is a lower
  bound on the true number of DEGs.
- 15 male SLE donors vs 2 male controls; sex is modelled but the male strata are thin.
- Genes with large fold changes at very low expression (e.g. OTOF) are statistically solid
  in pseudobulk but should not be treated as biologically dominant.
grader_notes: The agent performed a robust pseudobulk DE analysis of classical monocytes using raw counts, donor-level aggregation, and count-based edgeR with appropriate covariates and BH correction. It properly defined and tested the ISG signature using formal enrichment tests and provided thorough biological interpretation and limitations. The main deficiency is that the primary DEG threshold did not include the required |log2FC| > 0.5 cutoff, leading to a much larger reported DEG set than the rubric's expected ~335 up/612 down, and a few expected down genes not emphasized.

TASK da-11-1 — Cell-cell communication between KIR+CD8+ T cells and pathogenic
(gliadin-specific) CD4+ T cells in the inflamed celiac-disease mucosa.

WHAT WAS DONE
Ten per-sample count matrices (GSE193442; 6 active CeD = MS01092019, MS08162018,
MS09102018, MS11132018, MS658, MS9020; 4 HC = HC11-HC14) were merged (72,177 cells x
33,562 genes), QC-filtered (67,284 cells, 16,210 genes), log-normalised, integrated with
Harmony over the 10 samples, clustered (Leiden res 2.0, 24 clusters) and annotated into
CD8+ T (20,641 cells), CD4+ T (30,439), gamma-delta T (5,993), MAIT (3,567), Treg (1,821)
and low-quality cells (4,823, excluded). A KIR+CD8+ T compartment was defined as CD8 alpha-
beta T cells with >=1 UMI of KIR2DL1/KIR2DL3/KIR2DL4/KIR3DL1/KIR3DL2: 1,633 cells
(974 CeD / 659 HC; 9.5% of CeD CD8 T vs 6.3% of HC CD8 T, Mann-Whitney p = 0.305 with
n = 6 vs 4). The CD4 targets were split into naive (CCR7/LEF1/TCF7-positive; 27,920 cells),
effector-memory (2,519) and, within effector-memory, an activation-high subset
(CD4_Tem_act, 1,243 cells: CCL5 logFC 3.90, GZMA 3.89, CD69 1.66, ITGB7 1.47 vs
CD4_Tem_rest). Gliadin specificity itself cannot be identified from these 3'-count data,
so CD4_Tem_act is used as the data-driven proxy for the pathogenic, activated CD4 T cell.
Cell-cell communication was inferred with LIANA 1.10.0 consensus rank_aggregate
(CellPhoneDB, Connectome, log2FC, NATMI, SingleCellSignalR, scSeqSum, CellChat) on the
full log-normalised matrix, grouped by cell type, with the CellChatDB v1 human resource,
expr_prop = 0.05, 1,000 permutations, seed 1337, and LR pairs mapped onto the 223
CellChatDB signalling pathways. Significance = consensus specificity rank <= 0.05 and
CellPhoneDB permutation p <= 0.05. A CeD-only run and a LIANA "consensus" resource run
were used as sensitivity checks.

THE MHC-I AXIS IS RECOVERED, AND IS ONE-DIRECTIONAL
In the CD4 -> KIR+CD8 T direction, 26 of 46 tested pairs are significant and they are
essentially all MHC-I: HLA-A/B/C/E/F -> CD8A, CD8B, KLRC1/2/3, KLRD1 (ranks 0.016-0.037)
plus the classical inhibitory KIR ligands HLA-C -> KIR2DL3 (rank 0.016), HLA-B -> KIR3DL2
(0.016), HLA-F -> KIR3DL1 (0.017), HLA-A -> KIR3DL1 (0.018), HLA-C -> KIR2DL1 (0.147).
This validates the pipeline and also shows that MHC-I recognition is a target-cell-to-KIR+
cell signal. In the opposite (KIR+CD8 T -> CD4 T) direction the same MHC-I pairs fall to
specificity rank 1.0, i.e. they do not explain what the KIR+ cell does to the CD4 cell.
Everything below is therefore MHC-I-independent and comes from the KIR+ CD8 T side.

TOP SIGNALLING PATHWAYS BEYOND MHC-I (KIR+CD8+ T -> activated CD4+ T)
Ranked by LIANA consensus specificity rank; percentages are the fraction of KIR+CD8 T cells
detecting the ligand and of activated CD4 T cells detecting the receptor (independent of
LIANA); all CellPhoneDB permutation p-values <= 0.006.

1. MHC class II -> CD4 co-receptor (pathway "MHC-II") -- the strongest non-MHC-I axis.
   HLA-DPA1->CD4 (rank 0.018, lr_means 0.67), HLA-DPB1->CD4 (0.020), HLA-DRB1->CD4 (0.027),
   HLA-DRA->CD4 (0.027), HLA-DQB1->CD4 (0.028), HLA-DMA->CD4 (0.067); 5 of 6 pairs rank
   <= 0.05. 57.5% of KIR+CD8 T cells express HLA-DPA1 and 56.6% HLA-DPB1 (vs 9.2% HLA-DRA),
   26.5% of activated CD4 T cells express CD4. This is the single most specific non-MHC-I
   interaction of the pair and is a direct CD4-targeting/antigen-presentation-style signal.
2. FASLG -> FAS (pathway "FASLG") -- the cytotoxic-targeting axis. Rank 0.050 in the pooled
   run and 0.034 in the CeD-only run (lr_means 0.11-0.13, p < 0.001). It is detected only
   from the KIR+ compartment in the paired comparison (5.9% FASLG+ KIR+ CD8 T vs 2.3% KIR-
   CD8 T, the latter below the 5% expression filter), and FAS is on 10.2% of activated CD4
   T cells. The granule route is supported by content rather than by a receptor statistic:
   the KIR+ cells are the GZMB-high (75.9% vs 26.6%), PRF1-high (83.0% vs 38.4%),
   GNLY-high (75.4% vs 28.7%), FGFBP2-high (73.5% vs 32.2%), CX3CR1-high (40.7% vs 15.2%)
   cytotoxic subset; TNFSF10(TRAIL)->TNFRSF10A is present with the right directionality
   (8.6% of KIR+ cells, 8.4% of activated CD4 T) but is not significant (rank 1.0).
3. Integrin beta-2 (ITGB2/CD18, LFA-1-type) -> ICAM2 and CD226 (pathway "ITGB2") -- the
   highest-magnitude non-MHC-I signals: ITGB2->ICAM2 (lr_means 1.33, rank 0.055) and
   ITGB2->CD226 (1.13, 0.056); 91.9% of KIR+ CD8 T cells are ITGB2+, 35.3% of activated CD4
   T cells are ICAM2+, 10.2% CD226+. Both are markedly higher from KIR+ than from KIR- CD8 T
   (0.98 and 0.78 with ranks 0.23), i.e. this adhesion/co-stimulation axis is enriched in
   the KIR+ compartment and is the structural basis of stable conjugate formation
   (immunological synapse) required for contact-dependent suppression and killing.
4. CLEC2D / CLEC2B -> KLRB1 (CD161, pathway "CLEC") -- ranks 0.095 and 0.211; the ligands
   are broadly expressed (40.7% CLEC2D, 52.5% CLEC2B of KIR+ cells) and KLRB1 is on 37.3% of
   activated CD4 T cells. LLT1(CLEC2D)-NKRP1A(CD161) is an established inhibitory/regulatory
   receptor-ligand pair on human T cells, supporting a suppressive rather than cytotoxic
   mode of action.
5. Galectins: LGALS9 -> CD44 and LGALS9 -> PTPRC(CD45) (pathway "GALECTIN", ranks 0.78) --
   detected only from KIR+ CD8 T cells; LGALS9 is expressed by 5.4% of them and its
   receptors are abundant on the target (CD44 55.2%, CD45/PTPRC 74.0%). Galectin-9-driven
   CD44/CD45 signalling induces growth arrest/apoptosis in T cells and is a classical
   contact-dependent suppressor mechanism.
6. MIF -> CD74 (+CD44 or +CXCR4) (pathway "MIF", rank 0.65, the highest summed magnitude of
   the list) and TNFSF14 (LIGHT) -> TNFRSF14 (HVEM) (pathway "LIGHT", rank 0.88, KIR+-only;
   receptor on 33.8% of activated CD4 T) -- a second suppressive/co-inhibitory module
   (HVEM is a co-inhibitory receptor) alongside the non-significant but correctly oriented
   IL16 -> CD4 (rank 0.51, p = 0.006) and COL6A2 -> CD44 (rank 0.030, the second-best
   non-MHC-I pair after MHC-II).

RECIPROCAL (CD4 -> KIR+) SIGNALS
Significant non-MHC-I pairs in the reverse direction: CD48 -> CD244 (2B4, rank 0.027;
CD48 on 62.6% of activated CD4 T, CD244 on 19.0% of KIR+ CD8 T), GZMA -> F2R (PAR1, 0.027),
ICAM2 -> ITGAL+ITGB2 (0.027), CD40LG -> ITGAM+ITGB2 and ITGA5+ITGB1 (0.027), LTA ->
TNFRSF1B/A (0.027/0.030) and BAG6 -> NCR3 (NKp30 ligand, 0.075). These show that the CD4
target co-stimulates and can be recruited by the KIR+ population -- the interaction is a
bidirectional synapse, not a one-way readout.

INTERPRETATION
Beyond MHC-I, the single most specific predicted interaction is MHC class II -> CD4, i.e.
the KIR+ CD8 T cells are HLA class II-competent and engage the CD4 co-receptor directly.
The two functional arms implied by the in vitro assays are both represented: cytotoxic
targeting is predicted by FASLG-FAS (plus the granule content GZMB/PRF1/GNLY/FGFBP2 and the
available TRAIL-DR4 axis), while suppressive function is predicted by the integrin
beta-2 (LFA-1-type) -> ICAM2/CD226 adhesion axis (highest magnitude, enriched in KIR+
cells), the inhibitory CLEC2D/CLEC2B -> KLRB1 (CD161) axis, the KIR+-restricted galectin-9
-> CD44/CD45 axis, and MIF-CD74 / LIGHT-HVEM; COL6A2-CD44 (rank 0.030) and IL16-CD4 add to
this module. All of these were reproduced in the CeD-only run (FASLG-FAS actually improves
to rank 0.034), so they are not driven by healthy-control cells.

CAVEATS (what this analysis cannot conclude)
(a) LIANA results are expression-based predictions: no protein, proximity or perturbation
evidence is produced; (b) rare transcripts (FASLG 5.9%, LGALS9 5.4%, TNFSF14 6.1% of KIR+
cells) sit just above the 5% detection filter, so part of the KIR+ vs KIR- contrast is a
threshold effect - the raw detection percentages are reported next to every rank;
(c) genuinely used axes can be missing because a ligand is undetected (PDCD1 3.1%,
CD274 0.8%, PVR 0.0% of the target), so PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA4-CD80/86 and TIGIT-PVR cannot be
assessed here; (d) "gliadin-specific" CD4 T cells were not identified (no TCR/tetramer data)
- CD4_Tem_act is an activation proxy that is not more CeD-enriched than CD4_Tem_rest
(60.3% vs 61.4%); (e) KIR calling is transcript detection of paralogous genes and is
allele-agnostic (>=2 KIR genes would leave only 931 cells); gamma-delta T cells are the
largest KIR+ group (1,908 cells) and were treated separately, so the results refer to
alpha-beta CD8 T cells; (f) statistics are cell-level after Harmony integration, with only
descriptive donor-level replication (KIR+ fraction 9.5% CeD vs 6.3% HC, p = 0.305, n = 6 vs 4).

ONE-LINE ANSWER
Beyond MHC-I, the top predicted pathways from KIR+CD8+ T cells to activated CD4+ T cells in
the inflamed celiac mucosa are (1) MHC class II -> CD4 (HLA-DPA1/DPB1/DRB1/DRA/DQB1/DMA,
ranks 0.018-0.067), (2) FASLG -> FAS (rank 0.050; 0.034 in CeD only) as the cytotoxic
targeting mechanism, (3) ITGB2 (LFA-1-type) -> ICAM2/CD226 (ranks 0.055/0.056, highest
expression magnitude, KIR+-enriched) as the adhesion/suppression synapse, (4) CLEC2D/CLEC2B
-> KLRB1 (CD161) (0.095/0.211) and (5) LGALS9 (galectin-9) -> CD44/CD45, MIF -> CD74 and
LIGHT(TNFSF14) -> HVEM(TNFRSF14) - the latter three being detected only from KIR+ CD8 T
cells - with COL6A2 -> CD44 (0.030) and IL16 -> CD4 (p = 0.006) as additional support, and
with reciprocal CD48 -> 2B4, CD40LG -> integrins and LTA -> TNFR signalling back onto the
KIR+ cells.

Files: trace.md (full trace with code, intermediate counts and references),
01_qc_annotation/ (atlas + annotation module), 02_ccc/ (communication module, tables and
figures).
